title: A needle in my back? Consent for an urgent lumbar puncture in a 32-year-old woman with headache and fever in the emergency department
desc: In this station the candidate sees Jenny, a 32-year-old stay-at-home mother, in the emergency department. She has had a headache and fever since yesterday, and the ED registrar wants to do an urgent lumbar puncture. The candidate takes a focused history that screens for contraindications to lumbar puncture. They then examine for meningism, rash, papilloedema, focal signs, the source of infection and the skin of her lower back, and obtain informed consent for the lumbar puncture. In Part 2 the candidate reads her observations, bloods and CSF results and diagnoses bacterial meningitis (probably pneumococcal, from a left middle ear infection). They outline the steroid and antibiotic treatment already started, the vancomycin to add, admission, notification and follow-up.
focus: Obtaining informed consent for an urgent lumbar puncture after screening for contraindications, then interpreting CSF and managing bacterial meningitis without delaying antibiotics
stem: You are an intern working in the emergency department of a metropolitan hospital. Jenny, a 32-year-old stay-at-home mother, came in this morning with a headache and fever. The ED registrar has assessed her briefly and plans to do an urgent lumbar puncture herself. She has asked you to see Jenny first, assess her, and explain the procedure and obtain her consent. The registrar will confirm consent with Jenny before she starts. Your role is to give Jenny the information and take her consent under the registrar's delegation.
tasks: Take a focused history from Jenny and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Then explain the lumbar puncture to Jenny and obtain her informed consent (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Jenny's observations, her blood results and her CSF results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Jenny, 32, a stay-at-home mother of two: Mia, 5, and Noah, 2. You feel awful. You are lying on the trolley with your eyes half-closed and the lights dimmed, and you wince when you move your head. Your mind is clear and you are fully alert, but you answer in short sentences. The registrar told you she needs to do "a test with a needle in your back", and you are nervous about it. The examiner gives the examination findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "My head is pounding... The other doctor said I need a needle in my back? I'm a bit scared about that."

The illness (give only when asked):

  • Headache: it started yesterday at about 4 pm and built up over a few hours. It did not come on suddenly and it did not feel like being hit on the head. It is all over your head, worst at the front and the back, and goes down into your neck. It is constant, 8 out of 10, and worse when you move your head or look at light. Paracetamol 1 g and ibuprofen 400 mg at 6 am hardly helped.
  • Fever: you were hot and shivering all night. Your home thermometer read 39.5 °C at 5 am.
  • Vomiting: twice this morning. You have kept down only sips of water.
  • Light: it hurts your eyes.
  • Neck: stiff and sore. You cannot put your chin on your chest.
  • Before this (only if asked about recent illness or infections): about a week ago you caught a cold from the kids, with a blocked nose. For 4 days your left ear has been sore and muffled. You did not see a doctor about it.

Say no if asked about: a rash or spots; confusion or drowsiness (Tom says you have been yourself, just very sick); fits; weakness, numbness or trouble speaking; double, blurred or lost vision; a sudden "thunderclap" start; a head injury; cough or shortness of breath; urinary symptoms or diarrhoea; recent travel; contact with anyone who has had meningitis.

Bleeding and procedure questions (give only when asked): you take no blood thinners or aspirin and have no bleeding problems. You do not bruise easily, and bleeding was normal after both births and after a wisdom tooth extraction. No back surgery or back problems. No rash or sores on your back.

Past medical history: otherwise well. Two normal vaginal births. With the first you had an epidural, which went fine. No diabetes, no problems with your immune system, no operations on your spleen, never on steroids.

Medicines: a Mirena (hormonal IUD) for 2 years, and the paracetamol and ibuprofen this morning. Nothing else.

Allergies: none known. You had local anaesthetic at the dentist and for the epidural with no problems, and you have had amoxicillin before without a reaction.

Pregnancy (only if asked): not pregnant as far as you know. You have the Mirena, and you had a light period about 3 weeks ago. You are not breastfeeding (Noah stopped at 1).

Vaccines (only if asked): you had all your childhood vaccines but are not sure about any as an adult. The kids are fully vaccinated.

Family history: nothing relevant.

Social history: you live with your partner Tom, an electrician, and the kids, who go to childcare 2 days a week. Tom drove you in and has taken the kids to your mum's. He will be back soon. You do not smoke, you rarely drink and you use no drugs.

Ideas, concerns and expectations:

  • Idea: "I thought it was a bad flu, but Tom got worried when I couldn't bend my neck."
  • Concerns: the needle ("Will it hurt? Could it paralyse me?") and the kids ("Could they catch whatever I've got?").
  • Expectation: you want to feel better and get home to the kids.

Questions to raise during the consent discussion (ask each one only if the candidate has not already covered it):

  • "Will it hurt?"
  • "Could the needle hit my spinal cord and paralyse me?"
  • "Do I have to have it? What happens if I say no?"
  • "Do I have to wait for this test before I get any treatment?"

How to respond: if the candidate uses jargon (for example "CSF", "intrathecal", "herniation"), say "Sorry, I don't understand." Agree to the procedure once it has been explained clearly and your questions have been answered. If asked to explain it back, give a simple summary: "A thin needle in my lower back to take some of the fluid around my brain and spine to look for infection. My head might ache afterwards."

Exam findings (examiner: give only when the candidate says what they are examining):

  • General inspection: unwell, flushed and lying still with her eyes half-closed. Photophobic. Alert and talking in full sentences.
  • Observations (triage, 10:05): temperature 39.2 °C, HR 124/min regular, BP 108/68 mmHg, RR 20/min, SpO2 97% on room air, capillary glucose 6.4 mmol/L. (The full chart is handed over in Part 2.)
  • Conscious state: GCS 15 (E4 V5 M6), oriented to time, place and person. No confusion.
  • Skin, full inspection including the trunk, limbs, palms, soles and conjunctivae: no rash, no petechiae or purpura. Warm peripheries, capillary refill 2 seconds. Dry mucous membranes.
  • Meningism: marked neck stiffness. Kernig's sign positive. Brudzinski's sign positive (if tested).
  • Fundoscopy: optic discs pink with sharp margins on both sides. No papilloedema. Spontaneous venous pulsations present.
  • Pupils and cranial nerves: pupils 4 mm, equal and reactive. Eye movements full with no double vision. Visual fields full. Face symmetrical. Other cranial nerves normal.
  • Limbs: no pronator drift. Tone, power (5/5), reflexes and sensation normal and symmetrical. Plantars flexor.
  • Ears (otoscopy): left tympanic membrane red, dull and bulging with no perforation or discharge. Right normal. No mastoid tenderness or swelling.
  • Throat, sinuses and chest: throat mildly red. Sinuses non-tender. Chest clear. Heart sounds dual with no murmur.
  • Lower back: skin intact with no infection, rash or broken skin over the lumbar spine. No deformity. Spine not tender.
  • Abdomen (if examined): soft and non-tender.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Jenny's identity, and explains the purpose of the consultation.

Communicates clearly and kindly: dims the light or acknowledges her pain, finds out what she already knows and wants to know about the procedure, avoids jargon (or explains it), and uses a simple picture or description of the spine and needle.
check.d: Do not award if unexplained jargon is used (CSF, herniation, intrathecal).

check.x: History
Characterises the illness:

kids.x: Headache: began yesterday at about 4 pm, built up over hours (not sudden), generalised and into the neck, 8/10, little relief from paracetamol and ibuprofen.
kids.d: Award only if the speed of onset is asked about.

kids.x: Associated features: fever and rigors overnight, vomiting twice, photophobia and neck stiffness.

check.x: Screens for features that call for a CT brain before lumbar puncture: drowsiness or confusion, seizures, focal weakness or numbness, visual disturbance, and immune compromise [all absent].
check.d: Award for at least three of these, including seizures and a focal deficit.

check.x: Screens for bleeding risk: anticoagulants or antiplatelets, a known bleeding disorder, easy bruising or abnormal bleeding [none].

Looks for a source and risk factors: recent ear, sinus or chest infection (finds the cold and 4 days of left earache), head injury, splenectomy or immune problems, contact with anyone who had meningitis, travel, and vaccination status.
check.d: Award if the left earache is found and at least two other risk factors are asked about.

check.x: Takes the background history:

kids.x: Allergies, including antibiotics and local anaesthetic [none; amoxicillin, dental local anaesthetic and an epidural tolerated].

Past history, medicines and who is at home: otherwise well, epidural in her first labour, Mirena, paracetamol and ibuprofen this morning; lives with partner Tom and two children (5 and 2) who attend childcare, now with her mother.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Mirena, light period 3 weeks ago, not breastfeeding.

check.x: Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: thought it was flu; fears pain and paralysis from the needle, and that the children could catch it; wants to get home to them.
check.d: Award if concerns are explored at any point, including during the consent discussion.

check.x: Examination
Asks for the observations and assesses conscious state [T 39.2 °C, HR 124, BP 108/68, GCS 15].
Inspects the whole skin for a non-blanching (petechial or purpuric) rash [none].
Examines for meningism: neck stiffness and Kernig's or Brudzinski's sign [present].
Performs fundoscopy for papilloedema [sharp discs, none].
Screens for a focal neurological deficit: pupils, cranial nerves, pronator drift, limb power and reflexes [normal].
Looks for a source: otoscopy [left tympanic membrane red, dull and bulging], plus throat, sinuses or chest.
Inspects the skin over the lumbar spine for infection or broken skin [intact].
Informed consent (Part 1)

Explains the indication in plain words: to sample the fluid around the brain and spine to look for infection, whether it is bacterial or viral (and for bleeding), because meningitis is life-threatening and needs urgent diagnosis and the right treatment.
Explains the procedure:

kids.x: Before: bleeding risk and signs of raised pressure have been checked; a scan first is needed only if those signs are present (and they are not).

During: lying on her left side, knees curled to chest; the lower back is cleaned and draped; local anaesthetic; a thin needle between the bones of the lower back, below where the spinal cord ends; pressure measured and a few millilitres collected; about 30 minutes; pressure and soreness rather than sharp pain; keep still.
kids.d: Award if the position, local anaesthetic and needle below the spinal cord are all explained.

kids.x: After: a small dressing, rest, observations, and staying in hospital for treatment.

check.x: Explains the benefits (confirms the diagnosis and targets the treatment and its length) and the alternatives (blood cultures alone are less informative; untargeted antibiotics), and what declining would mean.
Reassures her that antibiotic treatment will not be delayed to wait for the lumbar puncture or its results.
Explains the risks:

kids.x: Common: headache afterwards, worse on sitting or standing, which can last days; back soreness; the procedure may not succeed and need repeating.
kids.d: Award only if post-LP headache is included.

kids.x: Rare: infection, bleeding, nerve irritation causing leg pain, numbness or weakness, local anaesthetic allergy; very rarely brain herniation, which is unlikely because she has no signs of raised pressure.
kids.d: Award for at least three rare risks.

check.x: Confirms capacity and voluntary agreement: checks her understanding (teach-back), answers her questions (pain, paralysis, saying no), states she may decline or withdraw, gains consent, documents it on the consent form, and tells her the registrar will confirm before starting.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: persistent fever and tachycardia in the yellow zone (clinical review), with BP, SpO2 and conscious state maintained; a systemic inflammatory response to a serious infection (suspected sepsis), with no organ dysfunction or shock so far, and no signs of rising intracranial pressure.

Interprets the bloods: neutrophilia and a markedly raised CRP (bacterial infection); normal platelets and coagulation (no bleeding contraindication); normal renal function and lactate; serum glucose 6.4 for the CSF ratio.
Interprets the CSF:

kids.x: Turbid fluid with a raised opening pressure, a neutrophil-predominant white cell count, high protein and low glucose; calculates and interprets the CSF:serum glucose ratio (about 0.17); a bacterial profile.
kids.d: Award only if cells, protein and the glucose ratio are all interpreted.

kids.x: Gram-positive diplococci, which suggest Streptococcus pneumoniae.

check.x: Gives bacterial meningitis, most likely pneumococcal, as the diagnosis, with left acute otitis media as the probable source.

Names differentials, each with a feature for or against from this case: meningococcal disease, viral (enteroviral) meningitis, HSV encephalitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage, and brain abscess or subdural empyema.
check.d: Award for at least three, including meningococcal disease and viral meningitis, each justified.

check.x: Management
Confirms the antimicrobial treatment was given straight after the LP (within 60 minutes of arrival) and continues it:

kids.x: Dexamethasone 10 mg IV 6-hourly for 4 days (first dose just before or with the first antibiotic dose).
kids.d: Accept the timing without the exact dose.
Accept ceftriaxone without the exact dose.

kids.x: Adds vancomycin IV now because Gram-positive diplococci are seen (loading dose 25 to 30 mg/kg, about 1.75 to 2 g for 68 kg, then dosing guided by levels) until susceptibility is known; rationalises to benzylpenicillin if susceptible, 10 to 14 days in total; seeks infectious diseases advice.
kids.d: Accept vancomycin without the exact dose.

check.x: Supportive care and monitoring: IV fluids, analgesia, antiemetic, frequent observations with GCS, and escalation if she deteriorates.

Involves the right people: ED senior, admission under the medical or infectious diseases team, ENT review of the ear source; states that invasive pneumococcal disease is notifiable once the organism is confirmed (the laboratory notifies; inform the public health unit if advised).
check.d: Award for admission plus one of ENT review or awareness of notification.

check.x: Safety netting

Tells Jenny in plain words what to report to the nurse straight away while in hospital: a worsening headache, drowsiness or confusion, a fit, new weakness or numbness, a rash, or leg pain or numbness after the needle; and that a headache on sitting up after the LP is common and usually settles.
check.d: Award for at least three red flags.

check.x: Answers her question about the children: pneumococcal meningitis is not spread like meningococcal disease and contacts do not need antibiotics, but they should see a doctor urgently (or call 000) if they become feverish, drowsy or develop a rash.
Arranges follow-up: culture and susceptibility results followed up, a hearing test (audiology) before or soon after discharge, and GP review after discharge.
check.d: Award only if the hearing test is included.

part2.lead: Jenny agreed to the lumbar puncture. Bloods and blood cultures were taken at 10:10, and the ED registrar performed the lumbar puncture at 10:40. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV and ceftriaxone 2 g IV were given at 10:45, straight after the lumbar puncture (40 minutes after triage). Here are Jenny's observations, her blood results, and the CSF results that the laboratory phoned through at 11:00.
part2.patient:
• When the candidate explains the diagnosis, ask: "Is it the bad kind? Am I going to be OK?"
  • At the fourth question, after the examiner has put it, ask: "What about my kids? Do they need antibiotics too?"
  • Then ask: "My head feels worse when I sit up. Is that from the needle?"

handover.label: Observations (ED, this morning)
handover.result: Triage observations and repeat sets before and after the lumbar puncture, on room air.
handover.model:
• Read: temperature 39.1 to 39.4 °C and HR 122 to 126 regular, both in the yellow zone of the NSW adult chart. That calls for a clinical review, and the persisting yellow-zone values must be escalated. RR 20, SpO2 96 to 97% on room air and SBP 104 to 108 are in the white zone. She was alert throughout. Capillary refill 2 seconds, glucose 6.4.
  • For Jenny: a systemic inflammatory response to a serious infection (suspected sepsis): fever and tachycardia, with no organ dysfunction or shock so far (BP and conscious state maintained). There is no bradycardia, hypertension or drop in GCS to suggest rising intracranial pressure.
  • What it changes: antibiotics and dexamethasone are already running; continue them. Urgent senior review. Give IV fluids, and continue frequent observations with GCS, escalating to a rapid response if any value enters the red zone or her conscious state falls.

rows.note: After lumbar puncture; site dry; dexamethasone and ceftriaxone given 10:45

handover.label: Bloods (10:10)
handover.result: Venous bloods collected 10:10. Blood cultures: two sets collected 10:10, incubating, no growth to report yet.
handover.model:
• Read: WCC 21.6 with a neutrophilia of 19.2, CRP 210 and a raised fibrinogen (acute phase). Haemoglobin and platelets are normal, and INR and APTT are normal. Sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine and lactate are normal. Serum glucose 6.4.
  • For Jenny: a marked inflammatory response that fits a bacterial infection. Normal platelets and clotting confirm there was no bleeding contraindication to the LP. Renal function is normal, so standard antibiotic dosing applies. The normal lactate and BP mean no septic shock.
  • What it changes: the serum glucose taken alongside the LP allows the CSF:serum glucose ratio. The blood cultures need following up for the organism and its sensitivities.

handover.label: CSF analysis (lumbar puncture, 10:40)
handover.result: CSF collected by lumbar puncture at L3/4 at 10:40, three tubes. Opening pressure measured in the left lateral position. Gram stain phoned to the ED registrar at 11:00. Culture, susceptibilities and viral PCR to follow.
handover.model:
• Read: turbid CSF with an opening pressure of 30 cmH2O. White cells 2400, almost all polymorphs, with few red cells. Protein 2.4 g/L. Glucose 1.1 mmol/L against a serum glucose of 6.4 (ratio 0.17, which the candidate should calculate). Gram-positive diplococci on Gram stain.
  • For Jenny: a neutrophilic pleocytosis with high protein and a very low glucose ratio is a bacterial profile, not viral (lymphocytes, near-normal glucose) or TB. Gram-positive diplococci mean Streptococcus pneumoniae (meningococci are Gram-negative). With her left otitis media, this is pneumococcal meningitis. A raised opening pressure is common in bacterial meningitis. The few red cells argue against subarachnoid haemorrhage.
  • What it changes: continue the dexamethasone (it benefits pneumococcal meningitis) and ceftriaxone, and add vancomycin now until susceptibility is known. Plan 10 to 14 days of treatment. Rationalise to benzylpenicillin if the organism is susceptible. Contacts do not need prophylaxis.

ask: You are now calling the medical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Jenny, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Jenny now, here in the emergency department.
Jenny asks what happens next and whether her children need treatment. What would you tell her, and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: ED intern; Jenny, 32.
  • Situation: about 18 hours of progressive headache, fever, vomiting, photophobia and neck stiffness; febrile and tachycardic; CSF shows bacterial meningitis.
  • Background: a week of URTI with 4 days of left earache; otherwise well; no anticoagulants or immune compromise; no allergies; two young children.
  • Assessment: GCS 15, meningism, no rash, no papilloedema or focal signs, red bulging left eardrum. T 39.4, HR 126 (yellow zone), BP maintained. WCC 21.6, CRP 210, clotting normal. CSF turbid, polymorphs 2160, protein 2.4, glucose ratio 0.17, Gram-positive diplococci: likely pneumococcal meningitis from otitis media.
  • Recommendation: continue dexamethasone and ceftriaxone (given 10:45) and add vancomycin; admit; please review; follow up confirmation for notification.

Most likely: bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae. For: fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and vomiting, a bacterial CSF profile, Gram-positive diplococci, and left otitis media as the source. (The commonest causes of meningitis in adults are S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis and enteroviruses.)

  • Meningococcal disease: for: young children in childcare. Against: no rash; meningococci are Gram-negative.
  • Viral (enteroviral) meningitis: for: children with colds. Against: polymorphs, very low glucose, organisms seen.
  • HSV encephalitis: against: GCS 15, no confusion, seizures or focal signs.
  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage: against: gradual onset, fever, few red cells.
  • Brain abscess or subdural empyema: for: ear source. Against: no focal signs or papilloedema.

1. Continue dexamethasone 10 mg IV 6-hourly for 4 days and ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly (first doses given at 10:45, within 60 minutes of arrival, straight after the LP and before the CSF result).
  2. Add vancomycin now (Gram-positive diplococci) pending susceptibility (loading dose 25 to 30 mg/kg, then dosing guided by levels), with infectious diseases advice. Rationalise to benzylpenicillin if susceptible. Total 10 to 14 days.
  3. Supportive: IV fluids, analgesia, antiemetic; frequent observations and GCS; escalate if she deteriorates.
  4. Involve: ED senior; admit under the medical or ID team; ENT for the ear. Invasive pneumococcal disease is notifiable once the organism is confirmed (the laboratory notifies; inform the public health unit if advised).
  5. Follow up the blood and CSF cultures.

• Explain: a bacterial infection of the lining of the brain, probably spread from the ear; serious, but treatable; IV antibiotics in hospital for about 10 to 14 days.
  • Tell the nurse straight away: a worsening headache, drowsiness or confusion, a fit, new weakness or numbness, a rash, or leg pain or numbness after the needle.
  • Headache after the LP: worse sitting up and usually settles; tell staff if it is severe or lasts.
  • Children: this germ does not spread like meningococcus, so they need no antibiotics; but if they become feverish, drowsy or develop a rash, see a doctor urgently or call 000.
  • Follow-up: culture results, a hearing test, and GP review after discharge.

ddx.dx: Bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae
ddx.for: Fever, progressive headache, vomiting, photophobia and meningism after 4 days of left earache with a bulging left eardrum; a neutrophilic CSF with high protein, a glucose ratio of 0.17 and Gram-positive diplococci.
Fever, headache and neck stiffness in a young adult whose children attend childcare.
ddx.against: No rash anywhere, and the Gram stain shows Gram-positive diplococci, whereas meningococci are Gram-negative.

ddx.for: A recent viral illness passed on from her young children, with fever, headache and photophobia.
ddx.against: The CSF is neutrophil-predominant with a very low glucose ratio and visible organisms.
GCS 15 with no confusion, behaviour change, seizures or focal signs, and a bacterial CSF picture with organisms seen.

ddx.for: Severe headache with neck stiffness and vomiting.
ddx.against: The headache built up over hours rather than suddenly, she is febrile, and the CSF is turbid with only 4 red cells.

ddx.dx: Brain abscess or subdural empyema from the ear
ddx.for: An untreated left middle ear infection as a contiguous source.
ddx.against: No focal deficit, seizures, papilloedema or reduced conscious state, and no mastoid tenderness.

guide:
Part 1: the consent discussion is the core of this station (about 4 to 5 minutes). Expect a brief focused history (about 3 to 4 minutes) that screens the CT and bleeding contraindications, then a brief targeted examination (about 2 minutes). Accept a stated, briefly described examination. Give findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. Jenny raises her questions about pain, paralysis, saying no and treatment timing only if the candidate has not covered them. The consent items (20 to 25) are scored in Part 1. Concerns (item 10) can be credited if they come out during the consent discussion. A candidate who insists on a CT brain before the LP should be asked once, "Why?". Do not award item 21.1 unless they recognise that she has none of the features that require it (GCS 15, no papilloedema, focal signs or seizures, not immunocompromised).

Part 2: hand over all three results together and ask the four questions in order. Score items 27 to 31 from the ISBAR and diagnosis answers, items 33 to 35 from the management answer, and items 37 to 39 from the fourth question. Credit item 38 when the candidate answers Jenny's question about her children.

A high-performing candidate screens efficiently for raised intracranial pressure, bleeding risk and local infection. They check the fundi, the skin and the lower back, and find the ear source. They consent in plain language, with an honest description of the risks, and reassure her that treatment will not wait for the test. They confirm her understanding and document the consent. In Part 2 they calculate the CSF:serum glucose ratio and read the CSF systematically, and they name pneumococcus from the Gram stain. They confirm that dexamethasone and ceftriaxone were given straight after the LP, continue them and add vancomycin. They know that invasive pneumococcal disease is notifiable once confirmed, and they explain clearly that her children need no prophylaxis.

A borderline candidate launches into consent without checking contraindications, omits fundoscopy or the rash check, uses jargon, or lists the risks without the post-LP headache. In Part 2 they may suggest holding treatment until the culture is back, forget the dexamethasone, miss the vancomycin despite Gram-positive diplococci, or wrongly give her children antibiotics as if this were meningococcal disease.
explain:
Why Jenny needs a lumbar puncture, and why antibiotics must not wait for it

Fever, a progressive headache, vomiting, photophobia and neck stiffness are meningitis until proven otherwise. CSF is the only way to confirm the diagnosis, tell bacterial from viral, identify the organism and its sensitivities, and set the length of treatment. eTG is clear that antibiotics must not be delayed to perform a lumbar puncture or CT. Take blood cultures, then give empirical antibiotics and dexamethasone within 60 minutes of arrival. An LP done promptly before the first dose gives the best yield, but empirical therapy follows straight after it, without waiting for the CSF result. If the LP cannot be done straight away, treat first and do the LP later. In this station Jenny's first doses were given at 10:45, straight after the LP and 40 minutes after triage.

Contraindications: screen before you consent

  • Signs of raised intracranial pressure: papilloedema, a new focal deficit, new seizures, or a reduced or falling GCS. Immunocompromise is also an indication for a CT first. With raised pressure, an LP risks herniation (coning) of the cerebellum and brainstem. If these signs are present, treat first, then do a CT, and do the LP only if it is safe.
  • Bleeding risk: anticoagulants, a bleeding disorder, or a low platelet count.
  • Skin infection over the puncture site.
  • Haemodynamic instability: resuscitate first.

Jenny has none of these: GCS 15, sharp discs, no focal signs or seizures, normal immunity, no bleeding history, intact skin and a maintained BP. No CT is needed. A raised CSF opening pressure is common in bacterial meningitis. It does not mean a CT was needed, because the decision to scan rests on the clinical signs.

Informed consent for a lumbar puncture

Valid consent needs capacity, enough information, and a voluntary decision. Jenny is unwell but has a GCS of 15 and can understand, weigh and communicate a decision. The person performing the procedure is responsible for consent. They may delegate the discussion only to someone with enough knowledge of the procedure, and here the registrar confirms consent before she starts. Structure the discussion:

  • Indication: to look for infection of the fluid around the brain and spine, whether it is bacterial or viral, and for bleeding.
  • Procedure: lying on her left side, knees to chest; the back cleaned and draped; local anaesthetic; a thin needle between the lumbar vertebrae, below where the spinal cord ends; pressure measured and a few millilitres collected. It takes about 30 minutes and feels like pressure rather than sharp pain. Afterwards: a dressing, rest, observations, and treatment in hospital.
  • Benefits: confirms the diagnosis and targets the treatment.
  • Risks: commonly a post-LP headache (worse upright, can last days), back pain and failure needing a repeat. Rarely infection, bleeding, nerve irritation with leg pain, numbness or weakness, and local anaesthetic allergy. Very rarely herniation, which is unlikely without signs of raised pressure.
  • Alternatives: blood cultures alone (less informative) or empirical antibiotics without targeting. Declining risks misdiagnosis and untargeted treatment.
  • Check understanding with teach-back, use a picture, avoid jargon, confirm she can decline or withdraw, and document the consent.

Interpreting the CSF

BacterialViralTB
AppearanceTurbidClearClear or fibrin web
CellsHigh; polymorphsRaised; lymphocytesRaised; lymphocytes
ProteinHighNormal or mildly raisedHigh
Glucose ratioLow (under 0.4)NormalLow

Jenny's CSF is bacterial on every count. Her CSF:serum glucose ratio is 1.1/6.4, about 0.17. The Gram stain points to the organism: Gram-positive diplococci mean Streptococcus pneumoniae, whereas Neisseria meningitidis is a Gram-negative diplococcus. The commonest causes of meningitis in adults are S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis (often with a non-blanching rash) and enteroviruses. Pneumococcal meningitis often follows otitis media, sinusitis or pneumonia, and is more likely after splenectomy, with alcohol excess or with a CSF leak. Jenny's left otitis media is the likely source.

Management (eTG Antibiotic: meningitis)

  • Dexamethasone 10 mg IV 6-hourly for 4 days, with the first dose given before or with the first antibiotic dose, but never delaying the antibiotic. If antibiotics have already been given, dexamethasone may still be started up to 4 hours afterwards. It reduces death and neurological sequelae, including hearing loss, in pneumococcal meningitis.
  • Empirical therapy: ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly, or cefotaxime. When Gram-positive diplococci are seen, add vancomycin to ceftriaxone until susceptibility is known, with infectious diseases advice.
  • Directed therapy: de-escalate to the organism once susceptibilities are known (benzylpenicillin if the pneumococcus is susceptible). Treat for 10 to 14 days.
  • Supportive care: IV fluids, analgesia, antiemetics, and frequent neurological observations, escalating early for a falling GCS, seizures or shock.
  • Source: an ENT review of the ear.
  • Notification: invasive pneumococcal disease is notifiable once S. pneumoniae is confirmed from a sterile site by culture, PCR or antigen; a Gram stain alone does not meet the case definition. In NSW the laboratory notifies it. Close contacts of meningococcal disease need clearance antibiotics. Contacts of pneumococcal meningitis do not.

Safety netting and follow-up

In hospital, Jenny should tell staff at once about a worsening headache, drowsiness, confusion, a fit, new weakness, a rash, or leg pain or numbness after the LP. A post-LP headache is worse when upright and usually settles. Sensorineural hearing loss is the commonest lasting complication of bacterial meningitis, especially pneumococcal, so arrange a hearing test before or soon after discharge, followed by GP review. Her children need no antibiotics. They should be seen urgently (or 000 called) if they become feverish, drowsy or develop a rash.
points: Never delay antibiotics for a lumbar puncture or CT: take blood cultures, then give dexamethasone and ceftriaxone within 60 minutes of arrival, straight after the LP and without waiting for the CSF result.

Before an LP, screen for raised intracranial pressure (papilloedema, focal deficit, new seizures, falling GCS, immunocompromise), bleeding risk, infection over the site and haemodynamic instability. A CT comes first only if pressure signs are present.

Consent for an LP covers the indication, the procedure before, during and after, the benefits, the risks (post-LP headache commonest, herniation rare), the alternatives and what declining would mean, in plain language, with teach-back and documentation.
Bacterial CSF is turbid, with polymorphs, high protein and a CSF:serum glucose ratio under 0.4. Gram-positive diplococci mean pneumococcus; Gram-negative diplococci mean meningococcus.

Give dexamethasone before or with the first antibiotic dose. Add vancomycin when Gram-positive diplococci are seen, until susceptibility is known, then de-escalate to the organism; pneumococcal meningitis is treated for 10 to 14 days.

Invasive pneumococcal disease is notifiable once confirmed (in NSW the laboratory notifies), but contacts need no prophylaxis (unlike meningococcal disease). Arrange a hearing test after bacterial meningitis.
